intro: The first time you hold a real chef's knife, it feels heavier and longer than anything you have used at the table. That is the right moment to learn how to hold it, because the habits you build in the first week are the ones your hands will keep. A knife does exactly what your hands tell it. This unit is about telling it clearly: where to put your thumb, how to tuck your fingertips, where the tip goes, and what to do with the knife when you are not cutting.

You will learn the parts of the knife and why a sharp one is safer than a dull one. You will practice the pinch grip and the claw until they feel normal, then the rocking cut that turns a carrot into even coins. You will set up a station that cannot slide, carry a knife across a room without anyone flinching, and wash and store it so the next person's hand is safe too.

Then the cuts. Slice, dice in three sizes, mince, julienne and chiffonade all have names because each one does a different job in a dish. You will dice an onion, mince garlic and roll basil into ribbons, and you will finish with a timed practical where the grade comes from safety, correct sizes, even pieces and a clean board. By the end you will be able to read a recipe's cutting words and do exactly what they ask.
bigQuestion: How do you handle a chef's knife so that every cut is safe, even and the size the recipe asks for?

timeline.t: People chip stone into sharp flakes, the first knives, for cutting meat and plants
Metalworkers cast bronze blades that hold an edge longer than stone
Iron blades spread; iron can be hammered thin and sharpened again and again
Sheffield, England, is already known for its knives; a poet of the time mentions one
Table knives with rounded tips become common in Europe, keeping sharp points off the dinner table
Factories in Sheffield and Solingen, Germany, forge steel kitchen knives for ordinary homes
Fannie Farmer's cookbook gives exact amounts, so cuts and measures start to be written the same way
Stainless steel is developed in Sheffield; knives that resist rust follow
Cooking schools teach the classic named cuts: dice, julienne, brunoise, chiffonade
Color-coded boards and food-safety rules keep raw meat and ready-to-eat food on separate surfaces
You learn the pinch grip, the claw and the rocking cut, and pass a knife-cuts practical

words.d: the pointed front of the blade, used for piercing and fine cuts
the back corner of the edge nearest the handle, strongest for hard foods
the dull top of the blade, safe to touch and to push cut food with
holding the knife with thumb and first finger pinching the blade just in front of the handle
the guiding-hand shape: fingertips curled under, knuckles forward, thumb tucked
a slicing motion where the tip stays on the board and the handle rocks down and forward
straightening a bent edge on a steel rod, done often
grinding a new edge on a stone or tool, done rarely, by an adult
cubes: small 1/4 inch, medium 1/2 inch, large 3/4 inch
pieces smaller than a grain of rice so flavor spreads through a dish
matchstick strips, 1/8 inch by 1/8 inch and about 2 inches long
thin ribbons of leafy herbs made by stacking, rolling tight and slicing across

test.q: Which part of the knife should push chopped onion off the board?
test.why: The spine is dull and safe. Pushing with the edge dulls it and can cut you.

test.q: Why is a sharp knife safer than a dull one?
choices: It cuts with little force, so it does not slip
test.why: Dull edges need hard pushing, and hard pushing slips. Sharp edges go where you aim.

test.q: In the pinch grip, the thumb and first finger are
choices: on the blade just in front of the handle
at the end of the handle
test.why: Pinching the blade near its balance point gives the most control.

test.q: The safe shape for the guiding hand is
choices: the claw, fingertips curled and knuckles forward
a fist on top of the food
test.why: The blade rides against the knuckles and cannot reach tucked fingertips.

test.q: In the rocking cut, the part of the knife that stays on the board is
test.why: Tip down, handle rocks. Lifting the whole knife scatters food and cuts.

test.q: What goes under the cutting board?
choices: Nothing; a clean counter is best
test.why: A damp towel grips both surfaces so the board cannot slide.

test.q: A knife falls off the counter. You should
choices: step back and let it land
test.why: Never try to catch a falling knife. Let it land, then pick it up by the handle.

test.q: Where should a knife never go?
choices: In a guard in a drawer
In a sink full of soapy water
test.why: A knife hidden in water is found edge-first by the next hand.

choices: straightens a bent edge and is done often
grinds a new edge and is done rarely
test.why: Honing realigns the edge on a steel; sharpening grinds new metal and is an adult's job.

test.q: A small dice is a cube that measures
The steps for any dice are
test.why: Flat slabs first, stacked into sticks, then cut across into cubes.

test.q: Why do cooks cut vegetables to one even size?
choices: So the pieces cook at the same rate
test.why: Heat moves from outside in. Same size means same cooking time for every piece.

test.q: The root end of an onion is left on while dicing because
choices: it makes the onion sit flat
it holds the layers together until the last cut
test.why: Without the root, the layers slide apart under the knife.

choices: stacking leaves, rolling tight and slicing across
chopping leaves with a fast rocking motion
smashing leaves under the flat of the blade
test.why: Stack, roll, slice gives thin ribbons without bruising the leaf.

test.q: On the knife practical, which is worth the most points?
test.why: Safety is graded every moment. Speed is worth the least.

write.prompt: Write the steps for dicing one onion into medium dice, from picking up the knife to putting it away, and explain why each step is there. Include how you hold the knife, what your other hand does, and what happens to the knife and board at the end.
tips: Put the steps in order, starting with the damp towel and the hand wash.
Name the grip and the guiding-hand shape, and say which part of the knife stays on the board.
Say why the root end stays on and give the size of a medium dice in inches.
Finish with washing, drying and storing the knife, and say where it must never go.
Check your numbers: 20-second hand wash, 1/2-inch cubes.
